120. When a fluxion is a rational fraction having either of these forms

\[
\frac{x^m}{x^n-a^n}, \quad \frac{x^m}{x^n-2pa^n}
\]

we can always, by the application of a particular theorem in analysis, resolve its denominator into real factors of the first and second degrees. The theorem to which we allude is this. Let \(n\) be any positive integer, and let \(z\) denote any arch of a circle, of which the radius is unity, then

\[
\cos(z) = \sqrt{-1} \sin(z) = \cos(nz) = \sqrt{-1} \sin(nz).
\]

We proceed to prove this theorem. Because

\[
(\cos(z) + \sqrt{-1} \sin(z)) (\cos(z) - \sqrt{-1} \sin(z)) = \cos^2(z) + \sin^2(z) = 1.
\]

If we put \(\cos(z) = \sqrt{-1} \sin(z) = v\),

Then \(\cos(z) = \sqrt{-1} \sin(z) = \frac{1}{v}\);

Therefore taking the sum of these two equations,

\[
2 \cos(z) = v + \frac{1}{v}.
\]

Now by the arithmetic of sines, (Algebra, § 358.)

\[
2 \cos(z) = 2 (2 \cos(z) \times \cos(z) - 1),
\]

\[
2 \cos(z) = 2 (2 \cos(z) \times \cos(z) \times \cos(z) - \cos(z)),
\]

\[
2 \cos(z) = 2 (2 \cos(z) \times \cos(z) \times \cos(z) \times \cos(z) - \cos(z)),
\]

&c.

Therefore, substituting in the first of these equations \(v + \frac{1}{v}\) instead of \(2 \cos(z)\), we have
In like manner, substituting in the second equation, \( v + \frac{1}{v} \) instead of \( 2 \text{ cof. } x \), and \( v^2 + \frac{1}{v^2} \) instead of \( 2 \text{ cof. } 2x \), we have

\[
2 \text{ cof. } 3x = (v + \frac{1}{v})(v^2 + \frac{1}{v^2}) - (v + \frac{1}{v})
\]

\[
= v^3 + \frac{1}{v^3}.
\]

Proceeding in the same way with the third and following equations, we find

\[
2 \text{ cof. } 4x = v^4 + \frac{1}{v^4},
\]

\[
2 \text{ cof. } 5x = v^5 + \frac{1}{v^5};
\]

To that we may conclude in general that

\[
2 \text{ cof. } nx = v^n + \frac{1}{v^n};
\]

Hence we have this quadratic equation

\[
v^n - 2 \text{ cof. } nx \times v^n + 1 = 0,
\]

from which, by completing the square, we find

\[
v^n = \text{ cof. } n \pm \sqrt{(\text{ cof. }^2 n \pm 1)};
\]

therefore, by substituting for \( v \) the quantity it was put to represent, and observing that \( \sqrt{(\text{ cof. }^2 n \pm 1)} = \sqrt{(-\text{ fin. }^2 n \pm 1)} = \sqrt{-1 \text{ fin. } n \pm 1} \), we have

\[
(\text{ cof. } \pm \sqrt{-1 \text{ fin. } n \pm 1})^n = \text{ cof. } n \pm \sqrt{-1 \text{ fin. } n \pm 1},
\]

as was to be proved.

121. The function \( x^n = a^n \) is transformed to \( a^n(y^n = 1) \) by putting \( x = ay \), and to discover its factors, we must resolve the equation

\[
y^n = 1 = 0.
\]

The expression \( y = \text{ cof. } x + \sqrt{-1 \text{ fin. } x} \) satisfies this equation, by a very simple determination of the arch \( x \); for we have \( y^n = (\text{ cof. } x + \sqrt{-1 \text{ fin. } x})^n = \text{ cof. } n \pm \sqrt{-1 \text{ fin. } n \pm 1} \), and as by putting \( \pi \) to denote half the circumference, and \( m \) any whole number, we have (ALGEBRA, § 352)

\[
\text{ fin. } m\pi = 0, \text{ cof. } m\pi = \pm 1,
\]

where the sign \( \pm \) is to be taken, if \( m \) be an even number, but \( \mp \) if it be odd, we have only to suppose \( n \pm m\pi \), in order to obtain \( y^n = \pm 1 \).

That we may distinguish the case in which \( m \) is even,

from that in which it is odd, we shall write for the first \( 2m \), and for the second \( 2m + 1 \); we therefore make

\[
n \pm 2m\pi, \text{ and } n \pm (2m + 1)\pi,
\]

By the first hypothesis, we find

\[
y^n = \pm 1, y = \text{ cof. } \frac{2m\pi}{n} + \sqrt{-1 \text{ fin. } \frac{2m\pi}{n}},
\]

and by the second

\[
y = \text{ cof. } \frac{(2m + 1)\pi}{n} + \sqrt{-1 \text{ fin. } \frac{(2m + 1)\pi}{n}}.
\]

122. By means of the indeterminate number \( m \), each of these expressions for \( y \) furnishes all the values of which this quantity is susceptible, for we may take successively

\[
m = 0, m = 1, m = 2, m = 3, \text{ &c.}
\]

The first formula gives

\[
y = \text{ cof. } 0.\pi = 1
\]

\[
y = \text{ cof. } \frac{2\pi}{n} + \sqrt{-1 \text{ fin. } \frac{2\pi}{n}},
\]

\[
y = \text{ cof. } \frac{4\pi}{n} + \sqrt{-1 \text{ fin. } \frac{4\pi}{n}},
\]

&c.

It is evident that we shall always have different results as far as \( m = n - 1 \). If, however, we suppose \( m = n \); then we have \( y = \text{ cof. } 2\pi = 1 \), which is the same as the first of the values already obtained, and if we suppose \( m = n + 1 \), then (ALGEBRA, § 25.)

\[
\text{ Cof. } \frac{(2n + 2)\pi}{n} = \text{ cof. } \frac{(2\pi + 2\pi)}{n} = \text{ cof. } \frac{2\pi}{n},
\]

\[
\text{ Sin. } \frac{(2n + 2)\pi}{n} = \text{ fin. } \frac{(2\pi + 2\pi)}{n} = \text{ fin. } \frac{2\pi}{n},
\]

which is the same as the second value, and so on with respect to the others.

By this mode of proceeding we shall not only obtain the \( n \) roots of the equation \( y^n = 1 \), or \( y^n - 1 = 0 \), but, with a little attention, we shall discover that these roots may be arranged in pairs, by bringing together those that only differ in the sign of the radical \( \sqrt{-1} \); for since

\[
\text{ Cof. } (2\pi - p) = \text{ cof. } p, \text{ and } \text{ fin. } (2\pi - p) = \text{ fin. } p,
\]

it follows that

\[
y = \text{ cof. } \frac{(2n - 2m)\pi}{n} + \sqrt{-1 \text{ fin. } \frac{(2n - 2m)\pi}{n}}
\]

\[
= \text{ cof. } \frac{2m\pi}{n} - \sqrt{-1 \text{ fin. } \frac{2m\pi}{n}}.
\]

Hence it appears that we may comprehend all the roots of the equation \( y^n - 1 = 0 \) in the single expression

\[
y =
\]
The first and the last of the factors of the second degree are the squares of \( y - 1 \) and \( y + 1 \), factors of the first degree, each of which only enters once into the proposed function; it will therefore be necessary, when we employ the factors of the second degree, to reject the first and last, and take instead of them

\[
(y-1)(y+1)=y^2-1.
\]

The factors of the first degree of the function \( y^5-1 \) are

\[
y-1
\]
\[
y-(\text{cof. } \frac{2\pi}{n} \pm \sqrt{-1} \sin \frac{2\pi}{n})
\]
\[
y-(\text{cof. } \frac{4\pi}{n} \pm \sqrt{-1} \sin \frac{4\pi}{n})
\]

Those of the second degree are

\[
y^2-2y+1,
\]
\[
y^2-2y\text{ cof. } \frac{2\pi}{5}+1,
\]
\[
y^2-2y\text{ cof. } \frac{4\pi}{5}+1;
\]

but it is to be observed that the first factor of the second degree is the square of \( y-1 \), which enters only once into the proposed function.

123. When the function to be decomposed into factors is \( y^6+1 \), the formula

\[
y=\text{cof. } \frac{(2m+1)\pi}{n} \pm \sqrt{-1} \sin \frac{(2m+1)\pi}{n}
\]

which corresponds to that case (\$ 121.) is also susceptible of the double sign \( \pm \), provided we stop at the value of \( m \) which gives

\[
2m+1=n, \quad \text{or} \quad 2m+1=n-1,
\]

according as \( n \) is odd or even; hence it follows that

\[
m=\frac{n-1}{2}, \quad m=\frac{n-2}{2};
\]

the factors of the first degree are

\[
y-(\text{cof. } \frac{(2m+1)\pi}{n} \pm \sqrt{-1} \sin \frac{(2m+1)\pi}{n}),
\]

and those of the second

\[
y^2-2y\text{ cof. } \frac{(2m+1)\pi}{n}+1.
\]

When among these last there is found some which are squares, we must take only one of their simple factors, in the same way as in the two preceding examples.

When the function is \( y^5+1 \),

the factors of the first degree are

\[
y-(\text{cof. } \frac{\pi}{5} \pm \sqrt{-1} \sin \frac{\pi}{5}),
\]
\[
y-(\text{cof. } \frac{3\pi}{5} \pm \sqrt{-1} \sin \frac{3\pi}{5})
\]
\[
y+1;
\]
and those of the second,

\[ y^2 - 2y \cos \frac{\pi}{5} + 1, \]

\[ y^2 - 2y \cos \frac{3\pi}{5} + 1, \]

\[ y^2 + 2y + 1. \]

The function \( y^6 + 1 \) has for factors of the first degree

\[ y - (\cos \frac{\pi}{6} = \sqrt{-1} \sin \frac{\pi}{6}), \]

\[ y - (\cos \frac{3\pi}{6} = \sqrt{-1} \sin \frac{3\pi}{6}), \]

\[ y - (\cos \frac{5\pi}{6} = \sqrt{-1} \sin \frac{5\pi}{6}), \]

and those of the second,

\[ y^2 - 2y \cos \frac{\pi}{6} + 1, \]

\[ y^2 - 2y \cos \frac{3\pi}{6} + 1, \text{ or } y^2 + 1, \]

\[ y^2 - 2y \cos \frac{5\pi}{6} + 1. \]

124. Such functions as are of this form \( x^n + 2px^n + q \) may be treated in the same manner as those which consist of only two terms. By putting the function \( = 0 \), and resolving the equation which is thus produced, in the same manner as if it were of the second degree, we find the factors to be

\[ x^n + (p = \sqrt{(p^2 - q)}); \]

if \( p^2 > q \), the second term of these factors is real, and by making

\[ a^n = p = \sqrt{(p^2 - q)}, \]

we have the functions of the form

\[ x = a^n \]

to decompose into factors.

When \( p^2 < q \), then we put \( p = a^n, q = b^n, x = b^n y, \)

and the function becomes

\[ b^n y^{2n} + 2a^n b^n y^n + b^n \]

\[ = b^n(y^{2n} + 2a^n y^n + 1); \]

but the condition \( p^2 < q \), or \( a^n < b^n \), makes \( a^n < b^n \),

and \( a^n < b^n \), therefore \( a^n \) may be represented by the cosine of a given arch \( \delta \), and the proposed function will be reduced to

\[ b^n(y^{2n} + 2y^n \cos \delta + 1), \]

we have then only to resolve the equation

\[ y^{2n} + 2y^n \cos \delta + 1 = 0, \]

and we immediately find

\[ y^n = \cos \delta = \sqrt{-1} \sin \delta; \]

we now assume, as in § 121,

\[ y = \cos \delta = \sqrt{-1} \sin \delta; \]

then we find (§ 120),

\[ y^n = \cos n \delta = \sqrt{-1} \sin n \delta, \]

which expression for \( y^n \), being compared with its other value, gives

\[ \cos n \delta = \cos \delta, \sin n \delta = \sin \delta. \]

These relations will be satisfied if we suppose \( n \delta = 2m\pi + \delta \), \( m \) being any whole number whatever, for

\[ \cos(2m\pi + \delta) = \cos \delta, \sin(2m\pi + \delta) = \sin \delta; \]

we have therefore

\[ \delta = \frac{2m\pi + \delta}{n}, \]

\[ y = \cos \frac{2m\pi + \delta}{n} = \sqrt{-1} \sin \frac{2m\pi + \delta}{n}. \]

The factors of the first degree of the function

\[ y^n + 2y^n \cos \delta + 1 \]

will consequently be comprehended in this formula,

\[ y = \left\{ \cos \frac{2m\pi + \delta}{n} = \sqrt{-1} \sin \frac{2m\pi + \delta}{n} \right\}. \]

If \( p \) the coefficient of the second term of the proposed function be negative, the only change necessary is to make \( p = -a^n \), and to take the arch \( \delta \) greater than a quadrant.

Of the Fluents of Irrational Functions.

125. When a fluxionary expression involves irrational functions, we must endeavour either to transform it into another that is rational, or to reduce it to a series of irrational terms of this form \( A^n x^n \), and then, in either case its fluent may be found by the rules already delivered.

Let us take for example the fluxion \( \frac{(1 + \sqrt{x})x}{1 + \sqrt{x}} \).

It is evident that by putting \( x = z^6 \), all the extractions indicated by the radical signs may be effected, and the fluxion may be transformed to \( \frac{6z^5(1 + z^2 - z^4)}{1 + z^2} \), which, by dividing the numerator by \( 1 + z^2 \), may be otherwise expressed thus,

\[ -6(z^7 - z^5 + z^3 - z + \frac{1}{1 + z^2}). \]

The fluent of which is

\[ -6 \left\{ \frac{z^8}{8} - \frac{z^7}{7} + \frac{z^6}{6} - \frac{z^5}{5} + \frac{z^3}{3} \right\} + \text{const}. \]
We shall first consider such fluxions as contain the irrational function \( \sqrt{A + Bx + Cx^2} \), and which have necessarily one or other of these forms.

\[
X \cdot \sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)} = \frac{X}{\sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)}}
\]

\( X \) being put for any rational function of \( x \); and it may be remarked, that the latter form comprehends the former, which may be written thus:

\[
\frac{X \cdot \sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)}}{\sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)}} = \frac{X(A + Bx + Cx^2)}{\sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)}}
\]

and here the numerator of the fluxion is a rational function of \( x \).

Before we transform the expression \( \sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)} \) into another that is rational with respect to the variable quantity it contains, we shall put the quantity \( A + Bx + Cx^2 \) under this form,

\[
C \left( \frac{A}{C} + \frac{B}{C} x + x^2 \right)
\]

and, in order to abridge, we shall put

\[
C = c^2, \quad \frac{A}{C} = a, \quad \frac{B}{C} = b,
\]

then we have

\[
\sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)} = c \sqrt{(a + bx + x^2)}
\]

Let us now assume \( \sqrt{(a + bx + x^2)} = x + z \), then, squaring both sides of the equation, we find \( a + bx = 2xz + z^2 \), hence we get \( x = \frac{a - z^2}{2z - b} \) and consequently

\[
\sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)} = c (x + z) = c \left( \frac{a - z^2}{2z - b} \right)
\]

\[
\dot{x} = \frac{2(a - bx + z^2)}{(2z - b)^2}
\]

By means of these values the fluxion \( \frac{X}{\sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)}} \) is transformed into another fluxion \( Z \dot{x} \), where \( Z \) denotes a rational function of \( z \), which is real when \( C \) or \( c^2 \) is positive; but as when \( C \) is negative \( c \) becomes imaginary, the fluxion \( Z \dot{x} \) which involves \( c \) becomes also imaginary.

In this case we have to consider \( \sqrt{(A + Bx - Cx^2)} \), and making

\[
C = c^2, \quad \frac{A}{C} = a, \quad \frac{B}{C} = b,
\]

it becomes \( c \sqrt{(a + bx - x^2)} \). The quantity \( x^2 - bx - a \) may always be decomposed into real factors of the first degree; let us represent these factors by \( x - \alpha \) and \( x - \alpha' \), then it is evident that

\[
a + bx - x^2 = (x - \alpha)(x - \alpha')
\]

Let us now assume

\[
\sqrt{(x - \alpha)(x' - x)} = (x - \alpha)x,
\]

then squaring both sides of the equation it becomes divisible by \( x - \alpha \), and we have \( \alpha' - x = (x - \alpha)x^2 \), from which we find

\[
x = \frac{a + z^2}{z^2 + 1}, \quad (x - \alpha) = \frac{(a - z^2)}{z^2 + 1},
\]

\[
\dot{x} = \frac{2(a - z^2)z}{(z^2 + 1)^2}
\]

values which render the proposed fluxion \( \frac{X}{\sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)}} \) rational.

Let us now take for example the fluxion \( \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)}} \); by applying to it the first of the preceding transformations it becomes \( \frac{-2z}{c(2z - b)} \), the fluent of which is \( \frac{1}{c} \ln(2z - b) + \text{const} \). Substituting now for \( z \) its value \( x + \sqrt{(a + bx + x^2)} \), and for \( a, b, \) and \( c \), the quantities they severally represent, the fluent becomes

\[
\frac{-1}{\sqrt{C}} \left[ \frac{B}{\sqrt{C}} - \frac{2x}{\sqrt{C}} \right] + \text{const}
\]

a result to which we may also give this form,

\[
\frac{-1}{\sqrt{C}} \left[ \frac{B}{\sqrt{C}} - \frac{2x}{\sqrt{C}} \right] + \sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)} + \text{const}
\]

+1. \( \frac{2}{\sqrt{C}} + \text{const} \)

By uniting the constant quantities into one, and observing that the radical quantity \( \sqrt{C} \) may have the sign prefixed to it, we have at last

\[
\int \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)}} \text{ equal to } \frac{1}{\sqrt{C}} \left[ \frac{B}{\sqrt{C}} + \frac{2x}{\sqrt{C}} + \sqrt{(A + Bx + Cx^2)} \right] + \text{const}
\]

Let us take for the second example \( \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(A + Bx - Cx^2)}} \). By employing the latter transformation of § 126, we have \( \frac{-2z}{c(z^2 + 1)} \), of which the fluent is

\[
- \frac{2}{c} \arctan(x) + \text{const}
\]

Substituting now instead of \( z \) its value \( \frac{\alpha' - x}{\sqrt{(x - \alpha)}} \) deduced from the equation \( \alpha' - x = (x - \alpha)x^2 \),

\[
5B \dot{x}
\]
and putting \( \sqrt{C} \) for \( c \), we get

\[
\int \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(A+Bx-Cx^2)}}
\]

equal to

\[
-\frac{2}{\sqrt{C}} \arctan \left( \frac{\sqrt{a'} - x}{\sqrt{(x-a)}} \right) + \text{const}.
\]

\( a \) and \( a' \) being the roots of the equation

\[
x^2 - \frac{B}{C} x - \frac{A}{C} = 0.
\]

Let us suppose that \( A = C = 1 \) and \( B = 0 \), then the proposed fluxion becomes in this particular case

\[
\int \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}}
\]

and the preceding formula gives for its fluent

\[
-2 \arctan \left( \frac{\sqrt{1-x}}{\sqrt{1+x}} \right) + \text{const.}
\]

for \( a \) and \( a' \) being the roots of the equation \( x^2 - 1 = 0 \), we must take \( a = -1 \), and \( a' = 1 \).

We may, however, give this fluent another form by proceeding thus: Let \( v \) be the arch whose tan.

\[
= \frac{\sqrt{1-x}}{\sqrt{1+x}}
\]

then \( \tan^2 v = \frac{1-x}{1+x} \), and \( x = \frac{1 - \tan^2 v}{1 + \tan^2 v} \)

\[
= \frac{2}{1 + \tan^2 v} - 1 = \frac{2}{\sec^2 v} - 1 = 2 \cos^2 v - 1,
\]

but \( 2 \cos^2 v - 1 = \text{cof. } 2v \) (Algebra, § 358.), therefore,

\[
x = \text{cof. } 2v.
\]

Put \( s \) for the arch whose sine is \( x \), and \( \pi \) for half the circumference, then \( x = \text{cof. } (\frac{\pi}{2} - s) \),

therefore \( 2v = \frac{\pi}{2} - s \), and since it has been shewn that

\[
\int \frac{\dot{s}}{\sqrt{(1-s^2)}} = -2s + \text{const.}
\]

therefore

\[
\int \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}} = -\frac{\pi}{2} + \text{const.}
\]

or, by including the arch \( \frac{\pi}{2} \) in the constant quantity,

\[
\int \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}} = s + \text{const.}
\]

This conclusion agrees with what has been shewn in § 59.

Instead of finding the fluent of

\[
\frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(A+Bx-Cx^2)}} = c \sqrt{(a+bx-x^2)}
\]

by first transforming it to a rational expression, we may reduce it directly to an arch of a circle by proceeding as follows. Put \( x = \frac{b}{2} \), then \( \dot{x} = \dot{s} \), and the fluxion is transformed to

\[
\frac{\dot{s}}{\sqrt{(a+\frac{b^2}{4}-x^2)}}
\]

again, put \( a + \frac{b^2}{4} = g^2 \), and \( x = g u \), then \( \dot{x} = g \dot{u} \), and this last fluxion is transformed to

\[
\frac{\dot{u}}{\sqrt{(1-u^2)}},
\]

the fluent of which is

\[
\frac{1}{2} \arctan (u) + \text{const.}
\]

Of the Fluents of Binomial Fluxions.

129. Let us now consider such fluxions as have this form

\[
x^{m-1} \cdot \frac{\dot{x}}{(a+bx^n)^q},
\]

and which are sometimes called binomial fluxions. We may here suppose \( m \) and \( n \) to be whole numbers,

without affecting the generality of the expression.

For if we had \( x^{m-1} \cdot \frac{\dot{x}}{(a+bx^n)^q} \), we may assume \( x = z^6 \),

then \( x = z^6 \cdot \frac{\dot{z}}{z^p} \), and the fluxion becomes \( 6z^7 \cdot \frac{\dot{z}}{(a+bx^n)^q} \).

We may also suppose \( n \) to be positive, for if it were negative, so that the fluxion were \( x^{m-1} \cdot \frac{\dot{x}}{(a+bx^{-n})^q} \) we have only to assume \( x = \frac{1}{z} \), and the fluxion is transformed to \( -z^{m-1} \cdot \frac{\dot{z}}{(a+zx^n)^q} \).

Let us inquire in what case the fluxion \( x^{m-1} \cdot \frac{\dot{x}}{(a+bx^n)^q} \) may become rational. Assume \( a + bx^n = z^p \),

then \( (a+bx^n)^q = z^p \), \( x^n = \frac{z^p - a}{b} \), \( x^m = \left( \frac{z^p - a}{b} \right)^n \),

and \( x^{m-1} \cdot \frac{\dot{x}}{nb} = \frac{q}{nb} \cdot \frac{\dot{z}}{z^p} \cdot \frac{z^p - a}{b} \);

hence the proposed fluxion is transformed to

\[
\frac{q}{nb} \cdot \frac{\dot{z}}{z^p} \cdot \frac{z^p - a}{b} = \left( \frac{z^p - a}{b} \right)^{m-1};
\]

this expression is evidently rational as often as \( \frac{m}{n} \) is a whole number.

There are yet other cases in which the fluxion may become rational, and which may be determined by assuming \( a + bx^n = z^p \), thus we have

\[
x^n = \frac{a}{u-b}, \quad x^m = \frac{a^m}{(u-b)^m},
\]

\[
x^{m-1} = \frac{-g a^m u^{p-1}}{n(u^q-b)^{m+1}},
\]

and because that \( (a-bx^n)^q \)

\[
= \frac{a^q u^p}{(u^q-b)^q}
\]

the fluxion \( x^{m-1} \cdot \frac{\dot{x}}{(a+bx^n)^q} \) is transformed to

\[
\frac{-g a^m u^{p-1}}{n(u^q-b)^{m+1}},
\]

an expression which is rational if \( \frac{m}{n} + \frac{p}{q} \) is a whole number.

130. As it is not possible, in every case, to express in finite terms the formula \( \int x^{m-1} \cdot \frac{\dot{x}}{(a+bx^n)^q} \), we may try to reduce it to its most simple case, as we have done.
done with respect to \( \int \frac{z}{(x^2 + b^2)^n} \) in § 114, which we have succeeded in reducing to \( \int \frac{z}{x^2 + b^2} \). To effect this reduction, we remark, that, since when \( u \) and \( v \) denote any functions of a variable quantity, the fluxion of \( uv \) is \( uv + vu \), (\$ 37.) therefore \( \int u \dot{v} = u \int v \dot{u} - \int v \dot{u} \). Now if we can decompose the expression \( x^{m-n} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p \) into two factors, such that we can find the fluent of one of them, then denoting that factor by \( v \), and the other by \( u \), the fluent of the proposed fluxion will be made to depend on that of \( vu \), which in some cases will be more simple than the proposed fluxion. That we may abridge a little the results, we shall write \( p \) instead of \( \frac{P}{q} \), so that \( p \) will represent any fraction; the proposed fluxion thus simplified in its form is

\[
x^{m-n} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p.
\]

Among the different ways of resolving this fluxion into two factors, we shall choose that which diminishes the exponent of \( x \) without the parentheses, we therefore write the fluxion thus

\[
x^{m-n} \cdot x^{m-n} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p,
\]

now the fluent of the factor \( x^{m-n} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p \) may always be determined, whatever be the value of \( p \), by § 108; let us denote this factor by \( v \), then

\[
v = \frac{(a + bx^n)^{p+1}}{(p+1)nb}, \quad \text{and} \quad u = x^{m-n},
\]

thus the formula \( \int u \dot{v} = u \int v \dot{u} - \int v \dot{u} \) give us \( \int x^{m-n} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p \) equal to

\[
\frac{x^{m-n} \cdot (a + bx^n)^{p+1}}{(p+1)nb} - \frac{m-n}{(p+1)nb} \int x^{m-n-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^{p+1}.
\]

But \( \int x^{m-n-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^{p+1} = \)

\[
\int x^{m-n-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p \cdot (a + bx^n) =
\]

\[
a \int x^{m-n-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p +
b \int x^{m-n-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p;
\]

Substituting now this last value in the preceding equation, and collecting into one the terms involving the fluent \( \int x^{m-n} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p \), we find

\[
\left(1 + \frac{m-n}{(p+1)nb}\right) \int x^{m-n-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p =
\]

\[
\frac{1}{(p+1)nb} \left\{ x^{m-n} \cdot (a + bx^n)^{p+1} - a(m-n) \int x^{m-n-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p \right\}
\]

hence at last we get

(A)

\[
\int x^{m-n} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p =
\]

\[
\frac{1}{b(pn+m)} \left\{ x^{m-n} \cdot (a + bx^n)^{p+1} - a(m-n) \int x^{m-n-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p \right\}
\]

It is easy to see that, as we have, by this formula, reduced the determination of the fluent of \( x^{m-n} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p \) to that of \( x^{m-n-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p \), we may reduce this last to that of \( x^{m-2n-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p \) by writing \( m-n \) in place of \( m \) in equation (A), then by changing \( m \) into \( m-2n \) we may reduce the fluent of \( x^{m-2n-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p \) to that of \( x^{m-3n-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p \), and so on.

In general, if \( r \) denote the number of reductions, we shall at last come to

\[
\int x^{m-rn-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p,
\]

and the last formula will be

\[
\int x^{m-(r-1)n-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p =
\]

\[
\frac{x^{m-rn} \cdot (a + bx^n)^{p+1}}{b(pn+m-(r-1)n)} -
\]

\[
\frac{a(m-rn)}{b(pn+m-(r-1)n)} \int x^{m-rn-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p.
\]

It appears by the last formula, that if \( m \) is a multiple of \( n \), then \( \int x^{m-rn} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p \) will be an algebraic quantity, for in that case the coefficient \( m-rn \) will be zero, and therefore the term containing \( \int x^{m-rn-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p \) will vanish. This result coincides with what we have already found, § 129.

131. We may also obtain a reduction, by which the exponent \( p \) will be diminished by unity. For this purpose it is sufficient to observe that \( \int x^{m-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^p \) is equal to

\[
\int x^{m-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^{p-1} \cdot (a + bx^n) =
\]

\[
a \int x^{m-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^{p-1} +
b \int x^{m+n-1} \cdot (a + bx^n)^{p-1},
\]

and that the formula (A) by changing \( m \) into \( m+n \), and \( p \) into \( p-1 \) gives
Substitute now this value in the preceding equation, we have

(B)

\[ \int x^{m-1} (a + bx^n)^p = \frac{x^m (a + bx^n)^{p+1}}{am} - \frac{b(m+n+np) \int x^{m+n-1} (a + bx^n)^p}{am}. \]

This formula diminishes the exponents without the parentheses, because \( m+n-1 \) becomes \( -m-n-1 \), when \( -m \) is substituted instead of \( m \).

To reverse formula (B) we first take

\[ \int x^{m-1} (a + bx^n)^p = \frac{x^m (a + bx^n)^p}{pna} + \frac{(m+n) \int x^{m-1} (a + bx^n)^p}{pna}; \]

Then, writing \( p+1 \) instead of \( p \), we find

(D)

\[ \int x^{m-1} (a + bx^n)^p = \frac{x^m (a + bx^n)^{p+1}}{(p+1)na} + \frac{(m+n+np) \int x^{m-1} (a + bx^n)^{p+1}}{(p+1)na}. \]

This formula answers the purpose we have in view, because \( p+1 \) becomes \( -p+1 \) when \( p \) is negative.

These formulas (A), (B), (C), (D), are inapplicable when their denominators vanish. This is the case with formula (A); for example, when \( m=-np \); but, in every such case, the proposed fluxion may have its fluent determined either algebraically or by logarithms.

132. It is evident, that if \( m \) and \( n \) were negative, the formulas (A) and (B) would not answer the purpose for which they have been investigated, because, in that case, they would increase the exponents instead of diminishing them. If, however, we reverse them, we shall find that they then apply to the case under consideration.

From formula (A) we get

\[ \int x^{m-n-1} (a + bx^n)^p = \frac{x^{m-n} (a + bx^n)^{p+1}}{a(m-n)} - \frac{b(m+n) \int x^{m-1} (a + bx^n)^p}{a(m-n)}. \]

Substitute now \( m+n \) in place of \( m \), and it becomes

(C)

\[ \int x^{m-1} (a + bx^n)^p = \frac{x^m (a + bx^n)^{p+1}}{am} - \frac{b(m+n+np) \int x^{m+n-1} (a + bx^n)^p}{am}. \]

133. Let the fluent be \( \int \frac{x^{m-1}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}, m \) being a whole positive number. Formula (A) immediately applies to this case, so that by putting \( a=1, b=-1, n=2, p=\frac{1}{2} \), we have

\[ \int \frac{x^{m-1}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \begin{cases} \frac{x^{m-2} \sqrt{1-x^2}}{m-1} \\ + \frac{m-2}{m-1} \int \frac{x^{m-3}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \end{cases} \]

or, substituting \( m \) in place of \( m-1 \),

\[ \int \frac{x^m}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \begin{cases} \frac{x^{m-1} \sqrt{1-x^2}}{m} \\ + \frac{m-1}{m} \int \frac{x^{m-2}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \end{cases} \]
Let us suppose, for example, that \( m = 1 \), then

\[
\int \frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = -\sqrt{1-x^2} + \text{const}.
\]

Let us now suppose that \( m = 3 \), then

\[
\int \frac{x^3}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l}
-\frac{1}{2}x^2 \sqrt{1-x^2} \\
+\frac{1}{2} \int \frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}
\end{array} \right.
\]

or, substituting for \( \int \frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \) its value,

\[
\int \frac{x^3}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = -\left( \frac{1}{3}x^2 + \frac{2}{3} \right) \sqrt{1-x^2} + \text{const}.
\]

If we suppose \( m = 2 \), then

\[
\int \frac{x^2}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l}
-\frac{1}{2}x \sqrt{1-x^2} \\
+\frac{1}{2} \int \frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}
\end{array} \right.
\]

But we have already found, § 128, that

\[
\int \frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \arcsin(x),
\]

therefore, putting \( A \) for \( \arcsin(x) \),

\[
\int \frac{x^2}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = -\frac{1}{2}x \sqrt{1-x^2} + \frac{1}{2}A + \text{const}.
\]

In the very same way we find that

\[
\int \frac{x^4}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \text{ is equal to }
\]

\[
-\left( \frac{1}{4}x^3 + \frac{3}{8}x \right) \sqrt{1-x^2} + \frac{3}{8}A + \text{const}.
\]

134. In the case of \( m \), a negative number, we must have recourse to formula (C), from which we find

\[
\int \frac{x^{m-1}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l}
-\frac{x^m \sqrt{1-x^2}}{m} \\
+\frac{m-1}{m} \int \frac{x^{m+1}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}
\end{array} \right.
\]

which formula, by writing \(-m\) instead of \(-m-1\), becomes

\[
\int \frac{x^m}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l}
-\frac{\sqrt{1-x^2}}{(m-1)x^{m-1}} \\
+\frac{m-2}{m-1} \int \frac{x^{m-2}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}
\end{array} \right.
\]

We cannot here suppose \( m = 1 \), for that value would render the denominator \(=0\); therefore, before we can apply this formula, it is necessary to investigate the fluent of \( \frac{x}{x \sqrt{1-x^2}} \). We may easily find it from § 126,

or otherwise thus, put \( x = \sqrt{1-x^2} \), \( \dot{x} = \frac{-x \dot{x}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \).

Therefore

\[
\frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \frac{-\dot{x}}{1-x^2} = \frac{-\dot{x}}{1+x} = \frac{-\dot{x}}{1-x}.
\]

The fluent of the right hand side of this equation is evidently (\$ 103.)

\[
-\frac{1}{2}(1+x) + \frac{1}{2}(1-x) = -\frac{1}{2}(1+x) + \frac{1}{2}(1-x);
\]

or, since \( \frac{1+x}{1-x} = \frac{(1+x)^2}{1-x^2} \), the same fluent may be expressed thus,

\[
-\frac{1}{2}(1+x)^2 = -\frac{1}{2}(1-x)^2;
\]

therefore, by substituting \( \sqrt{1-x^2} \) for \( z \), and \( x \) for \( \sqrt{1-x^2} \), we have

\[
\int \frac{x}{x \sqrt{1-x^2}} = -\frac{1}{2}(1+x) + \frac{1}{2}(1-x) + \text{const}.
\]

If we suppose \( m = 2 \), the formula becomes

\[
\int \frac{x^2}{x \sqrt{1-x^2}} = \frac{\sqrt{1-x^2}}{x} + \text{const}.
\]

If we suppose \( m = 3 \), then

\[
\int \frac{x^3}{x \sqrt{1-x^2}} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l}
-\frac{\sqrt{1-x^2}}{2x^2} \\
+\frac{1}{2} \int \frac{x}{x \sqrt{1-x^2}}
\end{array} \right.
\]

which expression, by substituting for

\[
\int \frac{x}{x \sqrt{1-x^2}} \text{ its value, becomes }
\]

\[
\int \frac{x^3}{x \sqrt{1-x^2}} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l}
-\frac{\sqrt{1-x^2}}{2x^2} \\
+\frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{1}{x} \sqrt{1-x^2} \right) + \text{const}.
\end{array} \right.
\]

Of Finding Fluents by Series.

135. We can always easily find an expression for the fluent \( \int X \dot{x} \), where \( X \) denotes any function of \( x \); when that function is expanded into a series, each term of which is some power of \( x \) multiplied by a constant quantity; thus suppose

\[
X = A x^n + B x^{n+1} + C x^{n+2} + \ldots
\]

then \( X \dot{x} \) is equal to

\[
Ax^n
\]
Inverse Method.

\[ A x^m + B x^{m+n} + C x^{m+2n} + \ldots + \text{&c.} \]

and taking the fluent of each term by § 101,

\[ \int X \dot{x} = \frac{A x^{m+1}}{m+1} + \frac{B x^{m+n+1}}{m+n+1} + \frac{C x^{m+2n+1}}{m+2n+1} + \ldots + \text{&c.} + \text{const.} \]

If in the development of \( x \) there be any term of this form \( \frac{A}{x} \), the fluent corresponding to that term will be

\[ A \ln x (\$ 103). \]

136. The most simple function of \( x \) that can be expanded into a series is \( \frac{1}{a+x} \), which becomes

\[ \frac{1}{a} - \frac{x}{a^2} + \frac{x^2}{a^3} - \frac{x^3}{a^4} + \ldots + \text{&c.} \]

Hence we find

\[ \frac{\dot{x}}{a+x} = \frac{\dot{x}}{a} - \frac{x \dot{x}}{a^2} + \frac{x^2 \dot{x}}{a^3} - \frac{x^3 \dot{x}}{a^4} + \ldots + \text{&c.} \]

and taking the fluents

\[ \int \frac{\dot{x}}{a+x} = \frac{x}{a} - \frac{x^2}{2a^2} + \frac{x^3}{3a^3} - \frac{x^4}{4a^4} + \ldots + \text{&c.} + \text{const.} \]

Now we know that \( \int \frac{\dot{x}}{a+x} = 1 \cdot (a+x) (\$ 57) \); therefore

\[ 1 \cdot (a+x) = \frac{x}{a} - \frac{x^2}{2a^2} + \frac{x^3}{3a^3} - \frac{x^4}{4a^4} + \ldots + \text{&c.} + \text{const.} \]

To find the value of the constant quantity we have only to make \( x=0 \), for then the equation becomes \( 1 \cdot a = \text{const.} \); therefore

\[ 1 \cdot (a+x) = 1 \cdot a + \frac{x}{a} - \frac{x^2}{2a^2} + \frac{x^3}{3a^3} - \frac{x^4}{4a^4} + \ldots + \text{&c.} \]

hence, if we subtract \( 1 \cdot a \) from each side, and observe that \( 1 \cdot (x+a)-1 \cdot a=1 \cdot \left( \frac{x+a}{a} \right)=1 \cdot \left( 1 + \frac{x}{a} \right) \), we get

\[ 1 \cdot \left( 1 + \frac{x}{a} \right) = \frac{x}{a} - \frac{x^2}{2a^2} + \frac{x^3}{3a^3} - \frac{x^4}{4a^4} + \ldots + \text{&c.} \]

From this conclusion we may deduce rules for computing the logarithms of numbers.

137. Let the fluxion be \( \frac{a \dot{x}}{a^2+x^2} \), which may be put under this form \( \frac{\dot{x}}{1+x^2/a^2} \), and which consequently belongs to the arch of which the tangent \( = \frac{x}{a} (\$ 6c.) \). By reducing \( \frac{a}{a^2+x^2} \) into a series, we find

\[ \frac{a}{a^2+x^2} = \frac{1}{a} - \frac{x^2}{a^3} + \frac{x^4}{a^5} - \frac{x^6}{a^7} + \ldots + \text{&c.} \]

Hence, multiply both sides by \( x \), and taking the fluent of each term, we get

\[ \int \frac{a \dot{x}}{a^2+x^2} = \arctan \left( \frac{x}{a} \right) + \text{const.} = \frac{x}{a} - \frac{x^3}{3a^3} + \frac{x^5}{5a^5} - \frac{x^7}{7a^7} + \ldots + \text{&c.} + \text{const.} \]

If we wish to deduce from this equation, the value of the least arch whose tangent is \( \frac{x}{a} \), it is necessary to suppress the arbitrary constant quantity; for when that arch \( = 0 \), then \( x=0 \); thus we have the arch whose tangent is \( \frac{x}{a} \) expressed by the infinite series

\[ \frac{x}{a} - \frac{x^3}{3a^3} + \frac{x^5}{5a^5} - \frac{x^7}{7a^7} + \ldots + \text{&c.} \]

Let \( \pi \) denote the circumference of a circle whose diameter is unity, or half the circumference of a circle whose radius is unity, then, as the sine of 30 degrees, or \( \frac{1}{2} \pi \), is \( \frac{1}{2} \), and its cosine \( \sqrt{1-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \), we have

\[ \tan \frac{\pi}{6} = \frac{\sin \frac{\pi}{6}}{\cos \frac{\pi}{6}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}. \]

Let \( \sqrt{\frac{1}{3}} \) be substituted instead of \( x \) in the above series, and \( a \) be supposed \( = 1 \), thus we get

\[ \frac{\pi}{6} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{3}} \times \left( 1 - \frac{1}{3 \cdot 3} + \frac{1}{5 \cdot 3^2} - \frac{1}{7 \cdot 3^3} + \ldots + \text{&c.} \right) \]

and therefore

\[ \pi = \sqrt{\frac{1}{12}} \times \left( 1 - \frac{1}{3 \cdot 3} + \frac{1}{5 \cdot 3^2} - \frac{1}{7 \cdot 3^3} + \ldots + \text{&c.} \right); \]

by taking the sum of about fifteen terms of this series, we shall find \( \pi=3.1415927 \). The determination of this number is of great importance in every branch of mathematics.

138. By proceeding with the fluxion \( \frac{x^m \dot{x}}{a^m+x^n} \) in the same manner as we have done with \( \frac{a \dot{x}}{a^2+x^2} \), we get

\[ \int \frac{x^m \dot{x}}{a^m+x^n} = \frac{x^{m+1}}{(m+1)a^m} - \frac{x^{m+n+1}}{(m+n+1)a^n} + \frac{x^{m+2n+1}}{(m+2n+1)a^n} + \ldots + \text{&c.} \]

This series proceeds by the positive powers of \( x \), or is an ascending series, but we may also expand \( \frac{1}{a^m+x^n} \) into a series proceeding by the negative powers of \( x \), and which will therefore be called a descending series. Thus because

\[ \frac{1}{a^n+x^n} \]
we have, after multiplying both sides by \( x^n \) and taking the fluents

\[
\int \frac{x^n}{x^n + a^n} = \frac{1}{(n-m-1)x^{n-m-1}} + \frac{a^n}{(2n-m-1)x^{n-m-1}} - \frac{(3n-m-1)a^n}{x^{n-m-1}} + \text{&c.} + \text{const.}
\]

This last series will be convergent when \( x \) is greater than \( a \), and at the same time \( m < n \), and \( n > 1 \). But besides, that it may contain algebraic terms only, it is necessary that none of the divisors \( n-m-1, 2n-m-1, 3n-m-1, \) &c., become \( = 0 \); this circumstance will take place as often as \( m+1 \) is a multiple of \( n \), and in which case

the series \( \frac{x^n}{x^n + a^n} = \frac{a^n}{x^{n-m}} + \text{&c.} \), which is the development of the fluxion, will contain a term of this form,

\[
\frac{a^n}{x}, \quad \text{the fluent of which is } a^n \cdot 1 \cdot x.
\]

If in this result we put \( m=2, n=0, \) and \( a=1 \), we get

\[
\int \frac{x}{1+x^2} = \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{3x^3} - \frac{1}{5x^5} + \text{&c.} + \text{const.}
\]

But although the expression \( \frac{x}{1+x^2} \) is the fluxion of the arch having \( x \) for its tangent, we must not conclude that this series is the development of that arch, for \( x \) being supposed \( = 0 \), each of the terms of the series becomes infinite.

The consideration of the constant quantity added to the fluent will remove this apparent difficulty, if we remark, that to know the true value of a series, it is always necessary to begin with the case in which it is convergent. Now the series

\[
\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{3x^3} - \frac{1}{5x^5} + \text{&c.}
\]

converges so much the faster as \( x \) is greater, and it vanishes when \( x \) is infinite; but in this extreme case the equation

\[
\arctan(x) = \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{3x^3} - \frac{1}{5x^5} + \text{&c.} + \text{const.}
\]

becomes simply \( \arctan(x) = \frac{\pi}{2} = \text{const.} \), where \( \pi \) denotes half the circumference of the circle; therefore, substituting this value of the constant quantity, we have

\[
\arctan(x) = \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{3x^3} - \frac{1}{5x^5} + \text{&c.}
\]

We may easily find an expression for the fluent of the rational fraction \( \frac{U}{V} \) (\$111.) by expanding the quantity \( \frac{U}{V} \) into a series, but the result thus obtained is in general very complicated, and seldom convergent; besides, this manner of finding the fluent is hardly of any use, since it may be expressed by means of arches of a circle and logarithms, both of which are readily obtained from the common trigonometrical tables.

139. The fluent of \( x^{m-n} \cdot (a+bx^n)^p \) is easily obtained by first expanding the quantity \( (a+bx^n)^p \) into a series by the binomial theorem, then multiplying each term of that series by \( x^{m-n} \), and taking the fluents of the results by §101. Thus we have

\[
\int x^{m-n} \cdot (a+bx^n)^p = \frac{p}{a^q} \left\{ \frac{x^m}{q} + \frac{p}{q} \frac{b}{a} \frac{x^{m+n}}{m+n} + \frac{p(p-q)}{1.2q^2} \frac{x^{m+2n}}{m+2n} + \frac{p(p-q)(p-2q)}{1.2.3q^3} \frac{x^{m+3n}}{m+3n} + \text{&c.} + \text{const.} \right\}
\]

This is an ascending series, but to get a descending series we must divide \( (a+bx^n)^p \) by \( x^q \) and multiply \( x^{m-n} \), the remaining part of the fluxional expression, by the same quantity, thus the fluxion is transformed to

\[
x^{m-n} \cdot (b+a \cdot x^{-n})^p
\]

the fluent of which, by proceeding as in the former case, is

\[
\frac{p}{b^q} \left\{ \frac{q^{m-n}}{mq+np} - \frac{p}{q} \frac{a}{b} \frac{q^{m-n}}{mq+(p-q)n} + \frac{p(p-q)}{1.2q^2} \frac{b^2}{mq+(p-2q)n} + \text{&c.} + \text{const.} \right\}
\]

either of these series may be employed if \( a \) and \( b \) are both positive, or \( q \) an odd number, but if \( q \) be an even number, the first formula becomes imaginary on account of the factor \( a^q \) if \( a^p \) be negative, and the same thing happens to the second formula if \( a^p \) be negative.

140. Let it be required to express by a series the fluent of \( \frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \). That we may develop the radical quantity \( \frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \) we put it under this form
Inverse Method.

\[(1-x^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}}, \text{ an expression which when expanded by the binomial theorem, is}\]

\[1 + \frac{1}{2}x^2 + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4}x^4 + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6}x^6 + \&c.\]

therefore, multiplying each term of this series by \(x\) and taking the fluent, we get

\[\int \frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}} = x + \frac{1}{2}x^3 + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 3}x^5 + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6}x^7 + \&c.\]

If we suppose \(x\) to denote the fine of an arch, then \(\sqrt{(1-x^2)}\) is its cosine, and \(\frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}}\) is the fluxion of the arch itself (\$59); therefore the series which we have just found expresses the length of the arch of a circle, radius being unity, and the fine of the arch \(x\).

If we suppose the series to express the smallest arch that corresponds to the fine \(x\), then, as when the fine of that arch \(=0\), the arch itself \(=0\), the series expressing the arch must vanish when \(x=0\), therefore we must suppress the constant quantity added to complete the fluent; or suppose it \(=0\). The same series has already been found by the direct method of fluxions in §72.

Let \(x\) denote the same as in §137, then, as the fine of 30 degrees, or of \(\frac{\pi}{6}\), is \(\frac{1}{3}\), we have, by substituting \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) instead of \(x\) in the preceding series, and multiplying both sides by 6,

\[x = 3 \left(1 + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 3 \cdot 2^3} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 5 \cdot 2^4} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 \cdot 7 \cdot 2^5} + \&c.\right)\]

by means of this series, which involves only rational numbers, we may compute (but with more labour), the value of \(\pi\) as before.

Suppose the fluxion to be \(\frac{x}{\sqrt{(ax-x^2)}}\), which may be otherwise expressed thus, \(x\sqrt{(1-\frac{x^2}{a})}\). By the binomial theorem \((1-x^2)^{-\frac{1}{2}} =\)

\[1 - \frac{x^2}{2a} - \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4}x^4 - \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6}x^6 - \&c.\]

Let each term of this series be multiplied by \(a^{\frac{1}{2}}x^{\frac{1}{2}}\), and the fluent taken by §101, thus we get \(\int x\sqrt{(ax-x^2)} =\)

\[a^{\frac{1}{2}} \left(\frac{2x^{\frac{3}{2}}}{3} - \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{2x^{\frac{5}{2}}}{5a} - \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4} \cdot \frac{2x^{\frac{7}{2}}}{7a^2} - \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6} \cdot \frac{2x^{\frac{9}{2}}}{9a^3} - \&c.\right) + \text{const.}\]

141. By resolving a fluxion into an infinite series, the object in view is to transform it into a series of other fluxions, each of which may have its fluent determined by known methods; but it is not always neces-

fary that the terms of the series should be each simply a power of \(x\) multiplied by \(x\) and constant quantities.

If for example we have this fluxion

\[\frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-e^2x^2)}}\]

in which \(e\) is supposed to denote a small constant quantity, we may expand \(\sqrt{(1-e^2x^2)}\) or \((1-e^2x^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}\) into a series, which will thus become

\[1 - \frac{1}{2}e^2x^2 - \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4}e^4x^4 - \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6}e^6x^6 - \&c.\]

and the fluxion \(\frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-e^2x^2)}}\) will be transformed to

\[\frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}} \left\{1 - \frac{1}{2}e^2x^2 - \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4}e^4x^4 - \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6}e^6x^6 - \&c.\right\}\]

the series will converge very fast when \(e\) is small, for that \(\sqrt{(1-x^2)}\) may be a real quantity, \(x^2\) must be less than 1. We must now multiply each term of the series by the common factor \(\frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}}\) and take the fluents, which being all contained in the general expression

\[\int \frac{x^m}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}}\]

will be found by §133. Thus, putting \(A\) to denote an arch of which \(x\) is the fine, we have

\[\int \frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}} = A + \frac{1}{2}e^2 \left\{\frac{1}{2}x^2 - \frac{1}{2}A\right\} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4}e^4 \left\{\frac{1}{4}x^4 + \frac{1}{2}x^2 - \frac{1}{2}A\right\} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6}e^6 \left\{\frac{1}{6}x^6 + \frac{1}{4}x^4 + \frac{1}{2}x^2 - \frac{1}{2}A\right\} + \&c.\]

Of the Fluents of such Fluxions as involve Logarithmic and Exponential functions.

142. Let it be required to find the fluent of \(x^m \log(x)\), where \(l.x\) denotes the Napierian logarithm of \(x\). In this case, as well as in some following examples, we shall have recourse to the principle already employed in §130, namely, that if \(v\) and \(x\) denote any functions of a variable quantity \(x\), then

\[\int v \cdot \frac{dx}{x} = v \cdot \log(x) - \int \frac{v}{x} \cdot dx.\]

Let us therefore assume \(x^{m+1} = v\), and \(l.x = z\), then, (\$101.), \(x^{m+1} = v\), and (\$57), \(z = x\), therefore, substituting
Part II.

Inverting Method.

Substituting these values of \( v \), \( x \), \( \dot{v} \), \( \dot{x} \) in the formula becomes

\[
\int x^m \dot{x} (1, x) = \frac{x^{m+1}}{m+1} - \int \frac{x^m \dot{x}}{m+1},
\]

or, since \( \int \frac{x^m \dot{x}}{m+1} = \frac{x^{m+1}}{(m+1)^2} + \text{const.} \),

\[
\int x^m \dot{x} (1, x) = x^{m+1} \left\{ \frac{1}{m+1} - \frac{1}{(m+1)^2} \right\} + \text{const.}
\]

Let us next suppose that the proposed fluxion is \( x^m \dot{x} (1, x)^n \). Put \( x^m \dot{x} = v \), and \( (1, x)^n = z \), then (\$101.)

\[
\frac{x^{m+1}}{m+1} = v, \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{n}{x} (1, x)^{-1} = z,
\]

therefore, substituting as before these values in the formula \( \int z \dot{v} = v - \int v \dot{z} \), we get

\[
\int x^m \dot{x} (1, x)^n = \frac{x^{m+1}}{m+1} (1, x)^{n+1} - \int \frac{n x^m \dot{x} (1, x)^{n-1}}{m+1}.
\]

It is evident, that by this formula the determination of the fluent of \( x^m \dot{x} (1, x)^n \) is reduced to that of \( x^m \dot{x} (1, x) \) which we have already found, and in like manner that the determination of the fluent of \( x^n \dot{x} (1, x)^3 \) is reduced to that of \( x^n \dot{x} (1, x)^2 \), and so on, from which it appears that the fluent of \( x^n \dot{x} (1, x)^n \) is expressible in finite terms when \( n \) is a whole positive number. The formula, however, will not apply when \( m = -1 \), because of the denominator \( m+1 = -1 + 1 = 0 \).

But in this case we have

\[
\int \frac{\dot{x}}{x} (1, x)^n = \frac{1}{n+1} (1, x)^{n+1} + \text{const.}
\]

If \( n \) be negative or fractional, the fluent of \( x^n \dot{x} (1, x)^n \) can only be expressed by an infinite series.

\$43. As an example of an exponential function, let it be required to find the fluent of \( x^n \dot{x} \). Here we may put \( \dot{v} = x^n \dot{x} \) and \( z = x^n \), then we have \( v = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} \), \$101, and \( z = (1, a) x^n \), (\$56.) therefore, substituting these values of \( v \), \( x \), \( \dot{v} \), \( \dot{x} \) in the formula \( \int z \dot{v} = v - \int v \dot{z} \), we get

\[
\int a^x x^n \dot{x} = \frac{a^x x^{n+1}}{n+1} - \int (1, a) a^x x^{n+1} \dot{x};
\]

therefore, substituting \( n = 1 \) everywhere instead of \( n \),

\[
\int a^x x^{n-1} \dot{x} = \frac{a^x x^n}{n} - \int (1, a) a^x x^n \dot{x};
\]

hence, bringing \( \int a^x x^n \dot{x} \) to stand alone one side of the equation

\[
\int a^x x^n \dot{x} = \frac{a^x x^n}{1, a} - \frac{n}{1, a} \int a^x x^{n-1} \dot{x}.
\]

If we suppose \( n = 1 \), then, observing that \( \int a^x \dot{x} = \frac{a^x}{1, a} \) (\$56.), \( \int a^x x^n \dot{x} = \frac{a^x x^n}{1, a} - \frac{a^x}{(1, a)^2} + \text{const.} \).

If \( n = 2 \), then

\[
\int a^x x^2 \dot{x} = \frac{a^x x^2}{1, a} - \frac{2}{1, a} \int a^x x \dot{x}.
\]

In this expression we substitute the value of \( \int a^x x \dot{x} \) just found, thus it becomes

\[
\int a^x x^2 \dot{x} = \frac{a^x x^2}{1, a} - \frac{2 a^x}{(1, a)^2} + \frac{2}{(1, a)^3} + \text{const.}
\]

Proceeding in this way we may find the fluent when \( n = 3 \), or when \( n = 4 \), or in general, when \( n \) is any integer number whatever, the number of terms in the fluent being in this case always finite; it is not so however when \( n \) is either negative or fractional.

Of the Fluents of such Fluxions as contain functions related to a circle.

\$44. Let us suppose that \( x \) is an arch whose sine is \( x \), and that it is required to find the fluent of \( x \dot{x} \). Put \( x^n \dot{x} = v \), then

\[
\int x^n \dot{x} = \int x \dot{v} = x - \int v \dot{x};
\]

but since \( \dot{v} = x^n \dot{x} \), we have \( v = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} \), \$101, and since \( x = \sin x \), we have \( \dot{x} = \cos x \), \( z = \sqrt{1-x^2} \) (\$59.), and therefore \( \dot{z} = \frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \); thus we have

\[
\int x^n \dot{x} = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} - \frac{1}{n+1} \int \frac{x^{n+1} \dot{x}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}};
\]

hence the determination of the proposed fluent is reduced to \( \int \frac{x^{n+1} \dot{x}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \) which we have already considered in \$133. By the same mode of reasoning we may determine the fluent when \( x \) denotes the cosine of the arch \( x \).

\$45. It appears from \$59, that \( n \) being put to denote any arch of a circle to radius unity, the fluxion of the sine of that arch is \( n \dot{x} \cos x \); therefore, on the contrary,

\[
\int \dot{x} \cos x = \frac{1}{n} \sin x + \text{const.}
\]

In like manner, from the formulas of \$59. and \$60., we find

\[
\int \dot{x} \sin x.
\]
\[ \int \dot{z} \sin^n z = -\frac{1}{n} \cos^n z + \text{const}. \]

\[ \int \dot{z} \cos^n z = \frac{1}{n} \tan^n z + \text{const}. \]

\[ \int \dot{z} \cot^n z = -\frac{1}{n} \cot^n z + \text{const}. \]

\[ \int \dot{z} \sec^n z = \frac{1}{n} \sec^n z + \text{const}. \]

\[ \int \dot{z} \csc^n z = -\frac{1}{n} \csc^n z + \text{const}. \]

146. By the second of these expressions we find the fluent of

\[ \dot{z} (A + B \sin z + C \sin 2z + \&c.) \]

to be

\[ A \dot{z} - B \cos z - \frac{1}{2} C \cos 2z + \&c. + \text{const}. \]

and from the first expression we find the fluent of

\[ \dot{z} (A + B \cos z + C \cos 2z + \&c.) \]

to be

\[ A \dot{z} + B \sin z + \frac{1}{2} C \sin 2z + \&c. + \text{const}. \]

147. It has been shewn in the Arithmetic of fines, (see Algebra, § 356.) that

\[ \sin^2 z = \frac{1}{2} (\cos 2z + 1), \]

therefore, by what has been shewn in § 145.

\[ \int \dot{z} \sin^2 z = \frac{1}{2} \int (\dot{z} \cos 2z + \dot{z}) \]

\[ = \frac{1}{2} (\dot{z} \sin 2z + \dot{z}) + \text{const}. \]

It has also been shewn that

\[ \sin^3 z = \frac{1}{4} (\sin 3z + 3 \sin z), \]

therefore, multiplying each term of this expression by \( \dot{z} \), and taking the fluents,

\[ \int \dot{z} \sin^3 z = \frac{1}{4} (\dot{z} \cos 3z - 3 \cos z) + \text{const}. \]

In the same manner may the fluent of \( \dot{z} \sin^n z \) be found, \( n \) being any positive integer number whatever.

Again, it has been shewn (Algebra, § 356.), that

\[ \cos^2 z = \frac{1}{2} (\cos 2z + 1); \]

therefore

\[ \int \dot{z} \cos^2 z = \frac{1}{2} \int (\dot{z} \cos 2z + \dot{z}) \]

\[ = \frac{1}{2} (\dot{z} \sin 2z + \dot{z}) + \text{const}. \]

and because

\[ \cos^3 z = \frac{1}{4} (\cos 3z + 3 \cos z) \]

therefore, multiplying by \( \dot{z} \), and taking the fluents,

\[ \int \dot{z} \cos^3 z = \frac{1}{4} (\dot{z} \cos 3z - 3 \cos z) + \text{const}. \]

and proceeding in this way we may find the fluents of \( \dot{z} \cos^n z \), \( n \) being any positive integer number.

148. The fluents of \( \dot{z} \sin^n z \) and \( \dot{z} \cos^n z \) may be expressed under another form, by proceeding as in § 142. Thus, beginning with \( \dot{z} \sin^n z \), and resolving it into \( \sin z \times \sin^{n-1} z \), if we put \( \dot{z} \sin z = v \), and \( \sin^{n-1} z = t \), we have by § 145, \( v = \cos z \), and (by § 26 and § 59) \( i = (n-1) \dot{z} \cos z \times \sin^{n-2} z \), therefore, substituting in the formula \( \int \dot{z} v = vt - \int \dot{z} v \), we have

\[ \int \dot{z} \sin^n z = -\cos z \sin^{n-1} z \]

\[ + (n-1) \int \dot{z} \cos^n z \sin^{n-2} z; \]

but \( \cos^2 z = 1 - \sin^2 z \), therefore \( \int \dot{z} \sin^n z \) is equal to

\[ -\cos z \sin^{n-1} z + (n-1) \int \dot{z} \sin^{n-2} z \]

\[ -(n-1) \int \dot{z} \sin^n z; \]

which expression, by bringing together the terms containing \( \int \dot{z} \sin^n z \) becomes

\[ \int \dot{z} \sin^n z = -\frac{1}{n} \cos z \sin^{n-1} z \]

\[ + \frac{n-1}{n} \int \dot{z} \sin^{n-2} z. \]

By giving particular values to \( n \) we have

\[ \int \dot{z} \sin^2 z = -\frac{1}{2} \cos z \sin z + \frac{1}{2} \dot{z} + \text{const}. \]

\[ \int \dot{z} \sin^3 z = -\frac{1}{3} \cos z \sin^2 z + \frac{2}{3} \dot{z} \sin z \]

\[ = -\frac{1}{3} \cos z \sin^2 z - \frac{2}{3} \dot{z} + \text{const}. \]

We may proceed in this way as far as we please, deducing the fluent of \( \dot{z} \sin^n z \) from that of \( \dot{z} \sin^1 z \), and the fluent of \( \dot{z} \sin^5 z \) from that of \( \dot{z} \sin^1 z \), and so on.

If in the general formula we substitute everywhere \( 2-n \) instead of \( n \), it becomes

\[ \int \dot{z} \sin^{2-n} z = \frac{1}{n-2} \cos z \sin^{1-n} z \]

\[ + \frac{n-1}{n-2} \int \dot{z} \sin^{1-n} z; \]
an expression which, by bringing \( \int \dot{z} \sin^{-n} z \) or \( \int \dot{z} \sin^n z \) to stand on one side of the equation, becomes

\[
\int \dot{z} \sin^n z = -\frac{1}{(n-1)} \cos z + \frac{n-2}{n-1} \int \dot{z} \sin^{n-2} z.
\]

This formula is not applicable to the case of \( n=1 \), because then each of the terms of the fluent is divided by \( n-1=0 \), and therefore becomes infinite. In order to obtain the expression for the fluent in this particular case, we proceed thus. It is evident that \( \frac{1}{\sin z} = \frac{1}{1-\cos^2 z} \); but \( \frac{1}{1-\cos^2 z} = \frac{1}{2(1-\cos z)} + \frac{1}{2(1+\cos z)} \)

as will be found by reducing the fractions to a common denominator, therefore \( \frac{1}{\sin z} = \frac{\sin z}{2(1-\cos z)} + \frac{\sin z}{2(1+\cos z)} \), and consequently,

\[
\int \dot{z} \sin z = \frac{1}{2} \int \dot{z} \sin z \left( \frac{1}{1-\cos z} \right) + \frac{1}{2} \int \dot{z} \sin z \left( \frac{1}{1+\cos z} \right);
\]

but if it be considered that the fluxion of \( \cos z \) is \( -\dot{z} \sin z \) (\$59.) it will appear by § 103 that \( \int \dot{z} \sin z \left( \frac{1}{1-\cos z} \right) = 1 \cdot (1-\cos z) \), and that \( \int \dot{z} \sin z \left( \frac{1}{1+\cos z} \right) = 1 \cdot (1+\cos z) \),

therefore

\[
\int \dot{z} \sin z = \frac{1}{2} \left[ 1 \cdot (1-\cos z) - \frac{1}{2} \left( 1 + \cos z \right) \right] + \text{const}.
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{1-\cos z}{1+\cos z} \right) + \text{const}.
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1+\cos z)}} + \text{const}.
\]

If in the general formula for \( \int \dot{z} \sin^n z \) we suppose \( n=2 \) we have

\[
\int \dot{z} \sin^2 z = \frac{\cos z}{\sin z} = -\cotan z + \text{const.}
\]

which agrees with what has been already observed (\$145.), and if we suppose \( n=3 \), then

\[
\int \dot{z} \sin^3 z = \frac{\cos z}{2 \sin^2 z} + \frac{1}{2} \int \dot{z} \sin z.
\]

In this way we proceed as far as we please, deducing \( \int \dot{z} \sin^4 z \) from \( \int \dot{z} \sin^3 z \), and so on.

\$149. If in the general formulas for \( \int \dot{z} \sin^n z \) and \( \int \dot{z} \cos^n z \) we substitute \( \frac{\pi}{2}-z \) instead of \( z \), (where \( \frac{\pi}{2} \) denotes a quadrant), and observe that

\[
\sin \left( \frac{\pi}{2}-z \right) = \cos z, \quad \cos \left( \frac{\pi}{2}-z \right) = \sin z,
\]

and that the fluxion of \( \left( \frac{\pi}{2}-z \right) \) is \( -\dot{z} \), we shall immediately obtain

\[
\int \dot{z} \cos^n z = \frac{1}{n} \sin z \cos^{n-1} z
\]

\[
+ \frac{n-1}{n} \int \dot{z} \cos^{n-2} z;
\]

and in like manner from the formula expressing the fluent of \( \int \dot{z} \cos^n z \) we deduce

\[
\int \dot{z} \cos^n z = \frac{1}{n} \left( \frac{1+\sin z}{1-\sin z} \right) + \text{const.}
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1+\sin z)}} + \text{const.}
\]

\$150. It has been shown in Algebra, § 357, that

\[
16 \cos^4 z \sin^3 z = \sin^5 z + \sin^3 z + 2 \sin z,
\]

therefore

\[
\int \dot{z} \cos^4 z \sin^3 z = \frac{1}{16} \left( \frac{1}{5} \cos^5 z - \frac{1}{3} \cos^3 z - 2 \cos z \right) + \text{const.}
\]

The same mode of finding the fluent will apply to any fluxion of this form \( \dot{z} \sin^m z \cos^n z \); or by resolving the fluxion into two parts, the determination of its fluent may be reduced to that of a fluxion in which the exponents \( m \) and \( n \) are less than in the proposed fluxion, by the method of proceeding already employed in § 148.

\$151. Let us now denote \( \sin z \) by \( x \), then \( \cos z = \sqrt{(1-x^2)} \) and since \( \cos z = \frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}} \) (\$59.) therefore \( z = \frac{x}{\sqrt{(1-x^2)}} \); these values being substituted in any function involving \( \dot{z}, \sin z \) and \( \cos z \) will immediately reduce it to an algebraic form. Thus for example, we shall have \( \dot{z} \sin^m z \cos^n z \) transformed to

\[
\dot{z} x^m (1-x^2)^{-\frac{n}{2}}
\]

an expression which may have its fluent determined by the formulas of § 133 and § 134.

**Sect. II. Application of the Inverse Method of Fluxions to the Resolution of Problems.**

To find the Areas of Curves.

\$152. It has been shown in § 61, that if the abscissa of a curve be denoted by \( x \), the ordinate by \( y \), and the area...
area by \( s \), then \( s = y \dot{x} \). Therefore the general formula expressing the area of any curve will be

\[
s = \int y \dot{x}
\]

Hence to find the area of any curve, we must either find from the equation of the curve the value of \( y \) in terms of \( x \), or else the value of \( x \) in terms of \( y \), and \( y \), and either the one or the other of these being substituted in the above formula, and the fluent found by the methods already explained, we shall have a general expression for the curvilinear area as required.

**Ex. 1.** Let it be required to find the area of any curve of the parabolic kind, of which, putting the abscissa \( AB = x \), and the ordinate \( BP = y \), the equation is

\[
y^n = ax^m
\]

Then we have \( y = a^{n/m} x^{m/n} \), and

\[
s = \int y \dot{x} = a^{n/m} \int x^{m/n} \dot{x}
\]

\[
= \frac{n}{m+n} a^{n/m} x^{m+n/n} + C,
\]

where \( C \) denotes the constant quantity that may be required to complete the fluent. As in the present case, it is required to find the area of the portion of the curve next its vertex, so that when \( x = 0 \), then \( s = 0 \), therefore also \( C = 0 \), and the area is simply

\[
\frac{n}{m+n} a^{n/m} x^{m+n/n}.
\]

If it be required to find the area comprehended between two ordinates \( PB, pb \), put \( AB = d \), then when \( s = 0 \), we have \( x = d \), therefore the general expression

\[
s = \frac{n}{m+n} a^{n/m} x^{m+n/n} + C
\]

becomes in this case

\[
s = \frac{n}{m+n} a^{n/m} d^{m+n/n} + C,
\]

hence \( C = -\frac{n}{m+m} a^{n/m} d^{m+n/n} \),

and consequently the area \( BP pb \), or \( s \), is equal to

\[
\frac{n}{m+n} a^{n/m} \left( x^{m+n/n} - d^{m+n/n} \right).
\]

When \( n \) is an even number, the expression for the area, viz., \( \frac{n}{m+n} a^{n/m} x^{m+n/n} \), may be considered as negative as well as positive, on account of the radical quantity \( \sqrt{x^{m+n/n}} \), which has then a twofold value, it may therefore have the sign prefixed to it; but in this case the same abscissa \( AB \) belongs to two branches of the curve \( APp \) and \( AP'p' \), as in fig. 19, No. 1, therefore the two values of the expression \( \frac{n}{m+n} a^{n/m} x^{m+n/n} \) may be considered as indicating the two areas \( APB, AP'B \), on each side of the axis, corresponding the one to the positive, and the other to the negative ordinates.

When the exponents \( m \) and \( n \) are both odd numbers,

\[
\frac{m+n}{m+n}
\]

the quantity \( x^{m+n} \) has only one sign, and remains always positive whatever be the sign of \( x \), but in this case one of the two branches of the curve has its abscissas and its ordinates negative at the same time (as in fig. 19, No. 2); it follows therefore that the areas corresponding to the negative abscissas and ordinates ought to be regarded as positive.

If \( n \) alone is odd, then the quantity \( x^{m+n} \) becomes negative at the same time as \( x \), but in this case the two branches of the curve are on the same side of the line in which the abscissas are taken (as in fig. 19, No. 3), and the ordinates remain always positive.

Upon the whole it may be concluded, that the area of a curve is positive when the abscissas and the ordinates have the same sign, and negative when they have contrary signs.

If we suppose \( m = 1 \), and \( n = 2 \), then the curve is the common parabola, the area of which from the general formula is found to be

\[
\frac{2}{3} a^{1/2} x^{3/2} = \frac{2}{3} xy;
\]

hence it appears that the parabola is \( \frac{2}{3} \) of its circumscribing parallelogram.

**Ex. 2.** Suppose the curve to be a circle. Put Fig. 20, \( AB = x, BP = y \), the diameter \( AD = a \), the area \( ABP = s \).

From the nature of the circle \( y^2 = a x - x^2 \), therefore \( y = \sqrt{(a x - x^2)} \), and

\[
s = \int y \dot{x} = \int \dot{x} \sqrt{(a x - x^2)}.
\]

In this case the fluxion is not of such a form as to admit of an algebraic fluent in finite terms, we must therefore have recourse to the method of series, but we have already found the fluent in this way in § 140, therefore, from the series there brought out we have

\[
s = \sqrt{a x} \left( \frac{2x}{3} - \frac{1}{2} \frac{2x^3}{5a} + \frac{1}{2} \frac{2x^3}{7a^3} - \frac{1}{2} \frac{2x^3}{9a^3} + \ldots \right)
\]

this expression does not require a constant quantity to be added to it, because when \( x = 0 \) we must also have \( s = 0 \).

If we suppose the arch \( AP \) to be \( \frac{\pi}{4} \) of the quadrant \( AE \), then it is known that \( PB = \frac{\pi}{4} \) the rad. \( AC = \frac{\pi}{4} a \), therefore, if we suppose the radius \( = 1 \), we have in this case \( BC = \frac{\pi}{4} \sqrt{3} \), and \( AB = 1 - \frac{\pi}{4} \sqrt{3} = 0.1339746 \) nearly. If this number be substituted instead of \( x \), and a few terms of the series computed, we shall find the area \( ABP = 0.452931 \); to this add the triangle \( CBP = \frac{1}{4} \times \frac{1}{4} = 0.2165063 \), and we have the sector \( ACP = 0.2617994 \), which number when multiplied by 3 gives \( 7853982 \) for the area of the quadrant. This number also expresses the area of a circle of which the diameter is 1.

**Ex. 3.** Suppose the curve to be an ellipse. Put Fig. 21,
the transverse axis \( AD = a \), the conjugate axis \( 2CE = b \), also \( AB = x \), \( BP = y \); then by the nature of the curve \( y = \frac{b}{a} \sqrt{(ax - x^2)} \), and \( s = y \dot{x} = \frac{b}{a} \sqrt{(ax - x^2)} \); but if a circle be described on \( AD \) as a diameter, and \( BP \) the ordinate of the ellipse be produced to meet the circle, it appears from last example that \( \dot{x} \sqrt{(ax - x^2)} \) is the fluxion of \( AQB \) the segment of the circle corresponding to the elliptic area \( APB \) or \( s \); therefore, putting \( v \) for the segment \( AQB \), we have

\[ s = \frac{b}{a} \dot{v} \text{ and } s = \frac{b}{a} v, \]

here the constant quantity \( c \) must be suppressed, because \( s \) and \( v \) must vanish together.

Hence it appears that the area of any segment of an ellipse is to the area of the corresponding segment of its circumfribing circle as the lesser axis of the ellipse is to the greater; therefore the whole ellipse must be to the whole circle in the same ratio.

**Ex. 5.** Let the curve be a hyperbola, of which \( C \) is the centre. Put the semi-transverse axis \( CA = a \), the semiconjugate axis \( CB = b \), \( BP = y \), the area \( APB = s \). From the nature of the curve \( y = \frac{b}{a} \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \), therefore

\[ s = \int y \dot{x} = \frac{b}{a} \int \dot{x} \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)}. \]

But it appears from formula B (\$131.) that

\[ \int \dot{x} \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} = \frac{a}{2} \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} - \frac{a}{2} \int \frac{\dot{x}}{\sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)}} \]

and again by \$127,

\[ \int \dot{x} \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} = 1. \left\{ x + \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \right\} + c, \]

therefore

\[ s = \frac{b}{2a} \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} - \frac{ab}{2}. \left\{ x + \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \right\} + c. \]

To discover the value of the constant quantity \( c \), we must consider that when \( x = a \), then \( s = 0 \), and in this extreme case the general equation just found becomes

\[ 0 = -\frac{ab}{2} l. a + c, \]

hence \( c = \frac{ab}{2} l. a \), and consequently, observing that

\[ -\frac{ab}{2} l. \left\{ x + \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \right\} + \frac{ab}{2} l. a = -\frac{ab}{2} l. \left\{ x + \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \right\}, \]

we get

\[ s = \frac{b}{2a} \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} - \frac{ab}{2}. \left\{ x + \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \right\}. \]

It immediately follows from this formula that

\[ \frac{b}{2a} \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} - s = \frac{ab}{2}. \left\{ x + \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \right\}. \]

but if a straight line be drawn from \( C \) to \( P \) so as to form the triangle \( CBP \), it is manifest that \( \frac{b}{2a} \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \) is equal to \( \frac{1}{2} CB \times BP \), that is, to the triangle \( CBP \), therefore the excess of the triangle \( CBP \) above the area \( s \), that is the hyperbolic sector \( CAP \), is equal to the logarithmic function

\[ \frac{ab}{2}. \left\{ x + \sqrt{(x^2 - a^2)} \right\}. \]

**Ex. 5.** Suppose the curve to be an equilateral hyperbola, that is a hyperbola whose axes are equal, and that it is required to find the curvilinear area \( DCBP \) comprehended between \( DC \), a perpendicular from \( D \) (a given point in the curve) to one of the asymptotes, and \( PB \), a perpendicular from any other point in the curve to the same asymptote.

Let \( A \) be the centre, put \( AC = a \), \( CD = b \), \( AB = x \), \( BP = y \), the area \( DCBP = s \). From the property of the asymptotes we have \( xy = ab \), and therefore \( y = \frac{ab}{x} \), hence (\$103.)

\[ s = \int y \dot{x} = \int \frac{ab}{x} \dot{x} = abl. x + c. \]

To find the value of \( c \), let us suppose \( x = a \), then \( s = 0 \), and the general formula becomes in this case

\[ 0 = abl. a + c, \]

and hence \( c = -abl. a \),

therefore

\[ s = abl. x - abl. a = abl. \frac{x}{a}. \]

If we suppose \( a = b = 1 \), then \( s = 1. x \), from which it appears that in this case the hyperbolic area \( DCBP \) represents the Napierian logarithm of the number \( x \); it was from the consideration of this property that the logarithms originally invented by Napier were called hyperbolical logarithms.

But the logarithms of any other system may also be represented by areas of the same hyperbola; for this purpose it is only necessary to determine the magnitudes of \( a \) and \( b \), so that \( \frac{b}{a} = M \), where \( M \) denotes the modulus of the system, thus we shall have \( ab = a^2 M \); and \( s = a^2 M l. \frac{a}{x} \), or, putting \( a = 1 \), \( s = M l. x \), an expression for the logarithm of \( x \) according to any system whatever of which the modulus is \( M \) (Algebra, §287.)

153. In some cases it is more convenient to refer a curve line to a fixed point than to an axis. Thus instead of expressing the nature of the circle by the equation \( y^2 = a x - x^2 \), where \( y \) denotes a perpendicular from any point of the curve upon \( a \) the diameter, and \( x \) the distance of that perpendicular from one end of the diameter, we may otherwise express it by the equation \( z = v \), where \( z \) denotes a variable arch of the circle reckoned from one end of its diameter, \( r \) its radius, and \( v \) the angle contained by a line drawn from the centre of the circle through the extremity of \( z \), which angle is measured by an arch of a circle having its radius unity.

The nature of the different conic sections may be defined in the same manner. Let \( P \) be any point in a conic section, of which \( F \) is one focus, and \( FA \) a part of the axis; let \( DC \) the directrix of the section meet \( FA \) in \( C \), join \( PF \), and draw \( PB \) perpendicular to the axis, and \( PD \) to the directrix; then from the nature of the curve (Conic Sections) \( PF \) has a given ratio to \( PD \), that is to \( FC - FB \); put \( FC = a \), \( FP = r \), the angle \( PFC = v \), and suppose \( PF : PD :: n : 1 \), then \( PF = n.PD = n.FC - n.FB \), hence observing that \( FB = FP \times \text{cof. } v \), we get \( r = a n - nr \text{ cof. } v \), and \( r = \frac{an}{1 + nr \text{ cof. } v} \) which equation expresses generally the nature of a conic section.

154. The formula which we have found for the fluxion of a curvilinear area, in § 61, is not immediately applicable when the nature of a curve is expressed in this way, we shall therefore investigate another formula suited to this particular manner of considering curves.

Let us suppose that \( APR \) is a curve the position of any point \( P \) of which is determined by \( PF \), its distance Fig. 26. from a given point \( F \), and the angle which \( PF \) makes with \( AF \) a line given by position. Let a circle be described on \( F \) as a centre with a rad. \( = 1 \), then \( FP \), as also the area \( FAP \), may be considered as functions of \( BD \) the arch of that circle which measures the angle \( PFA \). From \( F \) draw \( FP' \) to any other point \( P' \) of the curve meeting the circle \( BD \) in \( D' \). Put \( FP = r \), the area \( FAP = s \), the angle \( AFP \), or the arch \( BD = v \), then the area \( FP'P' \), and the arch \( DD' \), will be the corresponding increments of \( s \) and \( v \), therefore, § 21,

\[
\frac{\dot{s}}{\dot{v}} = \text{limit of } \frac{\text{area } FP'P'}{\text{DD' } \times \text{FD'}}.
\]

Here \( DD' \) the increment of \( v \) is multiplied by \( FD = 1 \), to render the terms of the ratio homogeneous. On \( F \) as a centre, with \( FP \) as a radius, describe an arch of a circle meeting \( FP' \) in \( Q \), then, as the sectors \( FDD' \), \( FPQ \) are similar, we have

\[
FE^2 : FP^2 :: FD \times DD' : FP \times PQ = 2 \text{ sect. } FPQ,
\]

hence \( DD' \times FD = \frac{2FD^2}{FP^2} \text{ sect. } FPQ = \frac{2}{r^2} \text{ sect. } FPQ \)

and \( \frac{\dot{s}}{\dot{v}} = \frac{r^2}{2} \times \lim_{\text{sect. } FPQ} \frac{\text{area } FP'P'}{\text{sect. } FPQ} \),

but the point \( P' \) being supposed to approach continually to \( P \), it is manifest that the limit of \( \frac{\text{area } FP'P'}{\text{sect. } FPQ} \) is unity, or 1, therefore

\[
\frac{\dot{s}}{\dot{v}} = \frac{r^2}{2}, \quad \text{and} \quad \dot{s} = \frac{1}{2} r^2 \dot{v}.
\]

\]

therefore,

\[
s = \int \frac{nr^2 \dot{v}}{2am} = \frac{nr^3}{6am}
\]

156. As the general expression for a curvilinear area $BCPD$ is $\int y \dot{x}$, where $x = AB$ the abscissa reckoned from a given point $A$ in the axis, and $y = BC$ the ordinate, it follows that $X$ being put to denote any function of a variable quantity $x$, the fluent of $X \dot{x}$ may always be exhibited by means of a curvilinear area. Thus let $CPD$ be a curve of such a nature that $AD$ and $DP$ the co-ordinates being denoted by $x$ and $y$, the equation of the curve is $y = X$, then, assuming any ordinate $BC$ as given by position, we have evidently

$$\int X \dot{x} = \text{area CBDP}.$$  

As the ordinate $BC$ (which is assumed as given by position) may be taken anywhere, the fluxion of the area being the same wherever it is taken, it appears, as has been already observed ($§ 101$) that the function $\int X \dot{x}$ may be considered as indeterminate, for it admits of innumerable values corresponding to any particular value of $x$, and in this respect it differs from an algebraic function, which for a given value of $x$ has always a determinate number of values. If however $x$ be supposed to increase from any determinate magnitude $a$, to any other determinate magnitude $a'$, then, taking the abscissa $AD = a$, and $AD = a'$, and drawing the ordinates $DP, dp$, we have

$$\text{when } x = a, \int X \dot{x} = \text{area CBDP},$$

and when $x = a', \int X \dot{x} = \text{area CBdp},$

therefore, while $x$ increases from $a$ to $a'$, or receives the increment $a' - a$, the function $\int X \dot{x}$ increases from area CBDP to area CBdp, and thus receives the increment area PD dp, which is of a determinate magnitude as the ordinates PD, pd have both a determinate position.

Hence it appears that in assigning the fluent of $X \dot{x}$, we only determine the change that takes place in the value of the function $\int X \dot{x}$ while $x$ passes from one particular value to another particular value.

157. As there are general and known methods by which an approximate value of any curvilinear area may be found, when a fluent is expressed by such an area, those methods may be applied to find an approximate value of the fluent. Let PD dp be a curvilinear area, supposed to represent the fluent $\int X \dot{x}$ between the limits of $x = AD$ and $x = A'd$. Conceive $DD'$ to be divided into a number of equal parts $DD', DD'', DD'$, and the ordinates $PD', PD''$ drawn, and the two sets of parallelograms $DE, DE', D'E', D'E''$ and $D'e, D'e', d'e'$ to be completed, the former constituting a rectilineal figure circumscribed about the curvilinear space $DPP'P''pd$, and the latter a rectilineal figure inscribed in that space; then as the circumscribed figure must necessarily be greater than the curvilinear space, that is, greater than

$$\int X \dot{x} \text{ taken between the limits of } x = AD \text{ and } x = A'a,$$

and the inscribed figure must be less, it follows that if we compute the areas of the circumscribed and inscribed figures we shall obtain two limits, the one greater, and the other less than $\int X \dot{x}$. And as by increasing the number of equal parts into which $DD'$ is divided we may bring the circumscribed and inscribed rectilineal figures as near to a ratio of equality as we please, it is always possible to find two limits which shall differ from each other, and consequently from $\int X \dot{x}$ (which lies between them) by less than any assignable quantity.

If we join $P, P', P'', p$, the tops of the ordinates, the rectilineal space formed by the trapeziums $DPP'D', D'P'P''D'', D''P''p$ will be more nearly equal to the curvilinear area, than the circumscribed rectilineal figure formed by the parallelograms $DE, DE', D'E', D'E''$; therefore the sum of those trapeziums being found, it will be equal to the fluent $\int X \dot{x}$ nearly.
